chapter_theme: The household life as the support of everyone else and as the fullest form of virtue. Having just exalted renunciants in chapter 3, the book now asks what they could gain by leaving home, and the commentators work hard to limit that challenge.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the household's service to all (41-42), how the householder does virtue (43-45), its superiority (46-49), and its fruit in the next life (50). He holds its fruit in this life, renown, for the end of the section.

41.reading: The one called a householder is the steady support, on their good path, of the three who keep their proper way.
41.nuance: The verse doesn't name the three, and what is meant by இயல்புடைய decides who is included.

positions.position: The three are the other life-stages, and he says Valluvar takes the first two from other people's doctrine.
positions.quote: இவருள் முன்னை இருவரையும் பிறர் மதம் மேற்கொண்டு கூறினார்.

positions.position: The three are one's parents, spouse and children.

42.reading: The householder is the support of those who have let go, those who have nothing and those who have died.
42.nuance: A single support reaches even the dead. Chapter 3 uses துறந்தார் for renouncers, so Parimelazhagar's different reading here gives the same word a very different sense.

positions.position: துறந்தார் are people abandoned by those who should support them, and இறந்தார் are those who die alone at the door.
துறந்தார் are renouncers who have given up caste and name.
They are ascetics, the hungry and the unprotected, so there is no duty to the dead here.

43.reading: To tend properly the five, namely ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself, is the chief duty.
43.nuance: The self is last on a list of duties. Parimelazhagar's reason is that one must exist in order to do any virtue, so self-care is a moral requirement. Kalaignar replaces ancestors and gods with memory of the dead and honour for those who live well.

44.reading: If a life fears blame and shares its food, its line never fails at any time.
44.nuance: Fear of blame comes before sharing because generosity can't launder what was wrongly got. Parimelazhagar gives a striking account of how merit and fault split in that case.

positions.position: If someone shares wealth that was wrongly taken, the merit goes to the owner and the sin stays with the sharer.
positions.quote: அறம் பொருளுடையார் மேலும், பாவம் தன் மேலுமாய் நின்று வழி எஞ்சும்

45.reading: If household life has love and virtue, these are its character and its fruit.
45.nuance: The verse makes the reward internal: the fruit of having love and virtue is having them. Parimelazhagar directs love to the wife and virtue to sharing, whereas Manakkudavar directs love to everyone and says no further reward is needed.

46.reading: If one conducts household life in the way of virtue, what would one gain by going off along the outside way?
46.nuance: The rhetorical question challenges chapter 3 directly. Everything depends on how far 'outside way' reaches.

positions.position: The outside way is only the forest stage, which leaves full renunciation out of the comparison.
The outside way is austerity in general, and the householder gets the fruit of austerity too.

47.reading: One who lives the household life according to its nature stands first among all who strive.
47.nuance: The verse doesn't say what they strive for, so the comparison group changes with each commentator.

positions.position: Those striving are ascetics trying to give up the senses, and the householder gets the result without such effort.
Those striving are people striving for wealth.

48.reading: A household life that keeps others on their way and doesn't itself slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance.
48.nuance: The word chosen, நோன்மை, is the ascetic's own virtue claimed for the householder. Parimelazhagar's reason is that the ascetic bears only their own pain, while the householder also bears that of others.

positions.position: The householder also endures the troubles that come upon others.

49.reading: What is called virtue is household life, and that too is good if there is nothing in it others can blame.
49.nuance: The whole verse turns on what அஃதும் points to. On one reading it is a rebuke to renunciants, and on another it is a condition on householders. Manakkudavar's explanation also shows a caste assumption of his own.

positions.position: 'That too' is renunciation, which is good only if it is free of hypocrisy.
positions.quote: ஏனைத் துறவறமோ எனின், அதுவும் பிறனால் பழிக்கப்படுவது இல்லையாயின்

positions.position: 'That too' is household life, and the blame in question would be a wife of low birth.
A blameless household life is what is honoured as the household dharma.

50.reading: One who lives on earth as life should be lived will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky.
50.nuance: வைக்கப்படும், 'will be placed', could mean a destiny or an estimation. Manakkudavar treats it as being honoured by all, while Parimelazhagar also expects actual godhood later on. The Tamil word for how to live, வாழ்வாங்கு, is left undefined.

links.note: In 23 those who weigh both paths and take up virtue here stand highest in the world. In 46 the householder has nothing to gain by leaving. Parimelazhagar resolves this by limiting 46 to the forest stage, but the verse doesn't state that limit.
Sharing food is a household duty here, and in 322 it becomes the chief of all that the authors have listed. What began as one household rule becomes the book's summary of virtue.

Here a well-lived earthly life earns a place among the gods. In 234 earthly renown goes further, so that the gods' world ceases to praise its own sages. Both measure human achievement against heaven and rate it highly.

source_issues: The Tamil of verse 50 in kg/core reads வான்உநற்யும், a typo for வான்உறையும் as Parimelazhagar's own text shows.
Manakkudavar's comment on verse 45 has OCR damage ('அவ் > ரண்டினையு', 'கொடுக்கவேண்டுமெ தும்'), and his comment on verse 49 ends with a stray '10'.
